In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of PPI in mice to differentiate between antipsychotics and to study the mechanism of antipsychotics.

the development of animal models of antipsychotic drug effects, which are relevant to the clinical situation, and with the identification of the neurobiological substrates underlying the behavioural deficits in schizophrenia.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PPI disruption induced by apomorphine is sensitive to typical antipsychotics, but not atypicals, in the rat and mouse.
the PPI model in the mouse is not useful for testing the antipsychotic properties of drugs.
the PPI model is not suitable for the screening of atypical antipsypchotic activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mouse PPI model might be a more sensitive model for testing atypical antipsycotics than the rat.
clozapine does not normalise apomorphine- or amphetamine-induced PPI deficits in mice.
the atypical antipshychotic clozapin is not effective in reversing PPI deficit induced by the dopamine agonist apomorphin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PPI disruption induced by apomorphine is not sensitive to clozapine in mice, and thus cannot be used as a model of clozapine-resistant schizophrenia in mice.
clozapine failed to normalise PPI deficits induced by systemic apomophine in the mouse.
the mouse might be more suitable than the rat for studying antipsychotic effects on PPI.
